html:
The bell-shaped burials culture, also called the cloche grave culture, was an early Iron Age culture of central and eastern Poland, from about the 500s to the 200s BCE. The map shows it from 500 BCE to 100 CE.

Its name comes from its graves. The dead were burned, and the urn holding the ashes was set in a pit and covered by a large upturned clay vessel shaped like a bell. Some covers sheltered more than one urn. Settlements were small farming villages.

Archaeologists still debate where it belongs. It appears where the late Lusatian culture had been, and it shares much with the Pomeranian culture spreading from the north. Many treat it as a southern variant of the Pomeranian culture rather than a separate people. Both were followed in the last centuries BCE by the Przeworsk culture.

Like the other cultures between the Oder and the Vistula in these centuries, it left no written records and no known name for its people. It sat between the Celts to the south, the Baltic peoples of Masuria to the northeast and the forest peoples further east.
